title: Cryptographic Agility
summary: Cryptographic agility is the property of a system that lets its algorithms, key sizes, protocol versions and certificate chains be replaced quickly without redesigning the application or recompiling firmware. It is achieved through indirection: algorithm selection is negotiated or configured rather than hard-coded, identifiers travel in the protocol or in metadata, and libraries expose a stable interface above changing primitives. Agility matters because deprecations arrive on someone else's schedule, whether from a broken hash function, a shortened key, a retired transport version, or the anticipated migration to post-quantum algorithms. It also matters because data already encrypted at rest cannot be re-protected unless the plaintext and the key remain available. Practical programmes start with a cryptographic inventory and automated discovery, then automate certificate and key lifecycle management, and stage migrations with both old and new algorithms supported so mixed peers keep working. The mistake is assuming agility arrives free with a library update, when the real obstacles are hard-coded cipher lists, undocumented protocols, and data encrypted once and never revisited.

beginner.definition: Cryptographic agility means being able to change the maths that protects your data without rebuilding everything. The maths, called algorithms, becomes old and unsafe over time. If your systems allow a swap, you can move to a newer method quickly. If the method is buried deep in the code, the change becomes slow and painful.
beginner.whyItMatters: Old methods are broken regularly, and future computers may one day break the methods we use today. A system that cannot change its method may have to be replaced, which costs time and money. Attackers look for old methods that are still switched on in hidden places. Being able to change quickly also helps when a library you use has a serious flaw. Planning for change is far cheaper than a rushed rebuild.
howItWorks: You list every place your systems use cryptography, including old devices, backups and third party links.
You store the chosen method as a setting or a label, never hard coded inside the program.
During a connection, both sides agree on a method from a list that they both support.
You keep two methods available during a change, so old and new peers can still talk to each other.
You monitor which methods are still in use, so you know when the old one can be switched off.
You test the change on a small group first. Keep a rollback plan, because a wrong setting can stop all traffic.
beginner.example: Think of an office that can change all its locks in one afternoon. The doors were built with standard fittings. The manager keeps a list of every door, cupboard and safe that uses a key. When a lock model is recalled, the change is quick and planned. A second office glued its locks into the doors. There, one recall closes the building for weeks. Cryptographic agility is the first office. Good design makes the change boring and fast.
takeaways: Keep a full list of where cryptography is used, because you cannot change what you cannot find.
Make the method a setting rather than hard coded logic, so a swap needs no rebuild.
Expect change as normal, and keep both old and new methods available during a migration.

objectives: Explain what cryptographic agility means and why organisations need it.
Describe the situations that force an algorithm or protocol change.
Identify design choices, such as configurable algorithm selection, that enable agility.
Explain what a cryptographic inventory is and why it comes first.
Outline how a cryptographic migration is staged and rolled back safely.
